chapters.label: Getting started
chapters.title: A first account you recognise
chapters.summary: Choose one useful purpose, record enough personal context to begin, and review the result in your own words. The relationship develops through experience and correction.
chapters.action: What would you like the first useful encounter to help you do? A short care introduction, a meaningful activity or a question for someone supporting you can provide a beginning.

chapters.label: Changing support needs
chapters.title: Support shaped by your life
chapters.summary: Younger onset dementia, disability and emerging aged care involve different lives and support arrangements. Begin with the person’s communication, abilities and chosen goals.
chapters.action: Choose a familiar activity and describe what makes it manageable or enjoyable. The relevant support team can then discuss a particular change and review what helped.

chapters.label: Identity and future wishes
chapters.title: Room to remember and to change
chapters.summary: Explore why an experience or preference matters. Earlier stories sit alongside present wishes, new friendships and possibilities still to come.
chapters.action: A simple question can open a useful conversation: when you say you miss home, which part of home do you mean? The person’s explanation leads the next step.

chapters.label: Memory palaces and downsizing
chapters.title: Keep the meaning of a place
chapters.summary: A familiar room, garden or object can lead back to a story. A place-based collection preserves selected photographs, recordings and their personal meaning through a move.
chapters.action: Begin with one place and one story. Give the item a recognisable name, its source and the person’s explanation, then try opening it in the format they expect to use later.

chapters.label: Moving home and into care
chapters.title: Carry your story into the next home
chapters.summary: Prepare a small, useful introduction for the receiving team. Earlier places remain part of a life that continues in a new room, with present routines and relationships.
chapters.action: Before moving day, agree what travels, who receives access and who can help open or correct the collection. Make the introduction short enough for a real care encounter.

chapters.label: Adult Genesis and wellbeing
chapters.title: Understand the adult research proposal
chapters.summary: The intensive adult Genesis design brings personal reflection, HBOT and Truth Engine research into a proposed programme. Each element needs its own purpose, assessment and evidence.
chapters.action: An actual research invitation needs to explain the activity, recording, clinical purpose, responsible team, alternatives and a practical way to stop. Everyday Aura support has its own introduction route.

chapters.label: People, consent and safety
chapters.title: People you can turn to
chapters.summary: Families, carers, providers, clinicians and researchers bring different responsibilities. A dependable offer makes those responsibilities and the person’s choices understandable.
chapters.action: Name who receives a concern, who follows it up, and where independent help is available. Choosing whether to join research remains separate from decisions about existing care.

chapters.label: Personal records and legal context
chapters.title: Useful access with clear boundaries
chapters.summary: Understand where information is held, who can use it and how to find or correct it. Legal learning helps prepare a clearer question and identify the responsible decision-maker.
chapters.action: Try recovering a selected story from a backup. Check the information and permission needed for the next encounter, including what happens if a device, supporter or provider changes.

chapters.label: Clinical development and evidence
chapters.title: Test a defined benefit
chapters.summary: A personal record, a clinical software function, HBOT and a Truth Engine task ask different questions. The proposed development route connects each claim with a suitable evaluation.
chapters.action: Describe one input, one output and the decision being supported. A clear purpose makes it possible to choose useful outcomes, examine errors and decide what the next study should test.

chapters.label: Care pathways and a local beginning
chapters.title: A practical place to begin
chapters.summary: Funding pathways, quality standards and local relationships shape what can actually be offered. A focused Queensland beginning would examine a defined need and the resources around it.
chapters.action: Set out who is paying, what is included, what support is needed and who is accountable. The Amity land proposal and a funded care or research service each require their own agreements.

chapters.label: Community, work and time
chapters.title: A whole life in the community
chapters.summary: Friendship, learning, creativity, rest and contribution belong alongside support needs. Wider Aura proposals explore voluntary reciprocity, shared enterprise and time throughout life.
chapters.action: Look for an invitation connected to the person’s interests and access needs. A welcoming event, creative project or skill shared with a neighbour can be worthwhile in its own right.

chapters.label: Developing the programme
chapters.title: Turn a useful purpose into a clear offer
chapters.summary: Prepare a demonstration, name the people and resources involved, and establish readiness before recruitment. The next step follows a review of the actual experience.
chapters.action: Bring one goal and your questions about what is currently available. Individuals, carers, providers, clinicians and research partners can each begin with the role they are considering.
